questions.q: Name two supporting characters from "The Cutting of My Long Hair" and two from "We Too are Human Beings."
questions.a: Correct: From Part I — Judewin, the paleface woman, the man at the end of the hall, the three young braves (any two). From Part II — Annan (elder brother), the elder from the street, the landlord, the landlord's man (any two). A wrong answer (e.g., naming Zitkala-Sa or Bama) reveals confusion between protagonist and supporting characters. Naming only generic "girls" or "people" shows inability to distinguish significant supporting figures from background.

questions.q: Explain why Judewin tells Zitkala-Sa "We have to submit, because they are strong." What does this reveal about Judewin's perspective?
questions.a: Judewin has internalized the powerlessness of their situation; she believes resistance is futile because the authorities hold all power. This reveals her perspective as one of resignation and survival through compliance. A wrong answer that calls her "practical" or "wise" misses the thematic contrast: she is a foil to Zitkala-Sa's rebellion, representing the psychological impact of systemic oppression.

questions.q: In "We Too are Human Beings," the elder carries the vadai packet by its string. Using this action, explain how Bama uses a supporting character to illustrate the practice of untouchability without directly stating it.
questions.a: The elder's refusal to touch the parcel — holding it by the string, bowing low — physically enacts the caste rule that upper-caste people would be "polluted" by contact. The landlord's casual acceptance normalizes this degradation. A wrong answer focusing only on Bama's initial amusement ("I wanted to shriek with laughter") misses the symbolic weight: the elder's body language makes invisible caste oppression visible.

questions.q: Compare the roles of Judewin (in Zitkala-Sa's narrative) and Annan (in Bama's narrative). How does each supporting character shape the protagonist's response to oppression?
questions.a: Judewin embodies submission ("We have to submit"), which provokes Zitkala-Sa to rebel ("I will struggle first!"). Annan embodies resistance through education ("If we study and make progress, we can throw away these indignities"), which inspires Bama to top her class. A wrong answer treating both as mere "advisors" fails to analyze their opposing influence: one reinforces the system, the other provides a tool to dismantle it.

questions.q: The paleface woman in "The Cutting of My Long Hair" is never named and described only by her actions. Is this an effective authorial choice? Justify your answer.
questions.a: Yes. By denying her a name and reducing her to "paleface woman" who watches, orders hair-cutting, and enforces rules, Zitkala-Sa dehumanizes the oppressor, turning her into a symbol of the assimilationist system rather than an individual. A wrong answer claiming it's "ineffective because we don't know her motives" misses the point: the system's facelessness is the horror.

questions.q: Write a short diary entry from Annan's perspective on the day he advises Bama to study hard. Include his thoughts on caste, education, and his hopes for his sister.
questions.a: A strong entry will reflect Annan's awareness of caste indignities (the landlord's man asking his street), his conviction that education is the only weapon ("study with care, learn all you can"), and his protective love for Bama. A poor entry will be generic ("I want her to do well") without anchoring in textual specifics like the library visits, the irrigation tank encounter, or the phrase "attach themselves to you."

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Character analysis of ______ characters involves examining the traits, actions, dialogues, and narrative functions of characters other than the protagonist to understand how they advance the plot, highlight the protagonist's qualities, and embody the text's central themes.

Fill in the blank: Imagine a friend who always says "just let it go" when you face unfairness, versus a sibling who says "fight back by excelling." In "Memories of Childhood," ______ characters play exactly these roles.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can identify all significant supporting characters in both autobiographical episodes, describe their key characteristics with specific textual evidence, explain their thematic function (e.g., as foils, symbols, or catalysts), and analyze how they shape the protagonists' responses to oppression.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Imagine a friend who always says "just let it go" when you face ______, versus a sibling who says "fight back by excelling." In "Memories of Childhood," supporting characters play exactly these roles.
